rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ghāshiyah pairs with al-Aʿlā in theme and assurance to the Prophet, while differing in address, reasoning, and breadth of treatment; it shows the Hereafter's outcomes as consequences of God's power, providence, and mercy.
rows.anchor: sounds assurance to the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending expands al-Aʿlā's brief reminder: the Prophet must communicate truth, not compel acceptance or pursue the obdurate, whose case he should leave to God.
rows.anchor: force others to accept it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–6 describe the fate of those heedless of the Hereafter, while verses 7–16 portray the success of those who live fearing it.
rows.anchor: A mention of the fate to be encountered by people who live in this world in complete disregard to the next world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation's signs display God's power, wisdom, mercy, and providence; a world without a justice day would deny these attributes and imply that God treats good and evil alike.
rows.anchor: It is the obvious outcome of His attributes of power, mercy, wisdom and providence that He one day bring about a day of justice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs make the warned reality manifest, so the Prophet should not despair over the stubborn; he only has to communicate the truth and entrust them to God.
rows.anchor: His responsibility is to only communicate the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is accountable only for communicating, not whether people accept; he should submit unwilling listeners to God, to whom they will return for reckoning.
rows.anchor: will not hold him accountable if people accept

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening question is rhetorical, expressing horror or majesty rather than seeking an answer.
rows.anchor: Questions expressed in such a style are not meant to elicit an answer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the address could be general, internal evidence identifies the Prophet as its addressee, confirmed by the sūrah's closing command to remind.
rows.anchor: the address in the verse can also be considered as general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāshiyah means something that engulfs and enshrouds; it describes Judgment Day because its all-embracing calamity will admit no escape.
rows.anchor: something which engulfs and enshrouds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though addressed to the Prophet, the news is meant to warn disbelievers who deny the Hereafter or assume they will fare even better than in this world.
rows.anchor: to inform the disbelievers who in the first place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding rhetorical question warns people to listen carefully; the Qur'an answers that many faces will be downcast and worn out on that Day.
rows.anchor: it was only meant to warn people that they should clearly listen to what is being sounded to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāshiʿa means downcast, ʿāmila tired from hard work, and nāṣiba worn out; sinners who must face Hell against their hopes will pale with fear.
rows.anchor: because of their misdeeds they would become pale with fear.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faces stand for people, but the wording points to their inward state because the face most clearly expresses it.
rows.anchor: used to refer to their inner state because it is the face

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description names the cause of the preceding anxiety; āniya means something boiling and seething.
rows.anchor: something which is boiling and seething.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sinners' anxious faces describe the moment they become certain they will be thrown into Hell, as in the cited passage from al-Qiyāmah.
rows.anchor: the anxiety of the sinners mentioned in this verse relates to the time

rows.speaker: people
rows.claim: Some understand this anxious state as occurring after entry into Hell; Islahi rejects that timing, since the cast sinners will be dragged on the fire and suffer more than anxiety.
rows.anchor: Generally, people have understood that this state of the sinners is the one which will result after they have been cast into Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍarīʿ is a thorny, poisonous bush that no animal will touch.
rows.anchor: a thorny and poisonous bush which no animal touches.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Illā is a severed exception: since ḍarīʿ is not edible, the point is that desperate sinners try it when no food is available, not that other Hell foods are excluded.
rows.anchor: is used here as a severed exception

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other Qur'anic passages also name zaqqūm and ghislīn as sinners' food, consistent with this verse's reference to forced, non-edible substances.
rows.anchor: these sinners will have to consume zaqq ūm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's inhabitants receive no food; instead they are made to swallow things that are not edible.
rows.anchor: can only be swallowed by the dwellers of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Food normally provides energy and relieves hunger, but Hell's provision does neither, forcing the agony of chewing and swallowing alone.
rows.anchor: The uses of food are two: to provide energy to the body and to satisfy the pangs of hunger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers' faces will shine with triumph, contrasting with the rejecters' dejection, fatigue, and frustration; al-Qiyāmah likewise describes faces awaiting their Lord's graciousness.
rows.anchor: their faces will glow and sparkle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are satisfied because their worldly labor's fruits lie before them: they have been generously rewarded and God's promises fulfilled.
rows.anchor: because the fruits of their labour will be before them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lofty gardens ringed by tall date palms matched Arab taste and appeared elegant while protecting against hot winds and floods.
rows.anchor: Arabs cherished gardens which were situated in lofty places

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's inhabitants blame one another; leaders and followers dispute responsibility, and followers demand double punishment for those who misled them.
rows.anchor: rightly guided. Leaders and their followers will have an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise's residents welcome one another with greetings and congratulations, meeting in bliss with love and sincerity.
rows.anchor: On the other hand, the dwellers of Paradise will welcome one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise has no worthless or sinful conversation, but greetings of peace fill the atmosphere.
rows.anchor: The atmosphere will resound with greetings of peace.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise's drink does not intoxicate or cause delirium, so its people retain control of their speech.
rows.anchor: will not make them lose their senses or make them delirious.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spring waters the orchard; singular mention does not imply it is the only spring, since al-Dahr describes multiple springs and distributaries of a different nature.
rows.anchor: The spring mentioned here is only the one used to water the orchard.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Descriptions across sūrahs usually elaborate brevity and sometimes reflect different ranks; the unseen is depicted in parables using the audience's familiar language and culture.
rows.anchor: this description is in the form of parables and an unseen world can only be described through parables

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lofty thrones follow the kings and nobles of Arabia as a model, while each resident's Paradise will be furnished to personal taste.
rows.anchor: Paradise will be according to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawb means a cup, mug, or goblet, and mawḍūʿa means well-arranged.
rows.anchor: which is the same as “a cup.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Namāriq are carpets and rugs arranged consecutively side by side, leaving no empty space.
rows.anchor: There will be no empty space.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zarābī are pillows and cushions scattered over carpets to provide comfortable seats wherever people wish to sit.
rows.anchor: They will act as comfortable seats to people wherever they want to sit.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs address people indifferent to the Hereafter, providing such plain evidence of providence, power, wisdom, and majesty that anyone open to truth cannot reasonably deny judgment.
rows.anchor: They are urged to reflect on these signs which bear evidence to the attributes of providence, power, wisdom and majesty of the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel is singled out as an everyday companion and servant, docile despite its size and able to serve people wherever they go.
rows.anchor: Why don’t they reflect on something which is their everyday companion?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel carries burdens like a desert ship, endures thirst and hunger, eats thorny bushes, obeys difficult tasks, and provides useful flesh, hide, milk, and dung.
rows.anchor: It carries all their burdens and is like a ship for them in desert journeys.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel's many uses and man's ability to tame it point to the Almighty's power and wisdom; reason supports creation and subjection by God rather than coincidence.
rows.anchor: sense and reason vouch for the second of these possibilities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God gave these undeserved comforts, people owe gratitude; ingratitude brings accountability and punishment.
rows.anchor: be held accountable before him and face punishment for denying all His favours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel represents all animals God placed in human service and on which livelihoods depend; every favor requires gratitude, implying a day to reward the grateful and punish the ungrateful.
rows.anchor: the grateful are rewarded for their gratefulness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the issue will be discussed at length in his tafsīr of al-ʿĀdiyāt.
rows.anchor: this issue shall be discussed at length.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky has no pillars, its age and distance are unknown, and even powerful telescopes reveal no flaw; sun, moon, planets, and stars sustain and adorn earthly life.
rows.anchor: such a limitless expanse was raised high without any pillars.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Creator can make the heavens, re-creating a human reduced to clay is no difficulty; the Qur'an elsewhere compares the two acts.
rows.anchor: He can make the heavens, will it be difficult for Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountains stabilize the earth, guide winds and clouds to bring rain, supply streams, hold treasures, and contain passages between peoples; these signs imply God's wisdom and accountability.
rows.anchor: They maintain the balance of the earth lest it should tilt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spread earth provides homes, crops, water, and livestock resources; its care raises whether God would ignore how people live or fail to distinguish gratitude from pride.
rows.anchor: placed them in a house that He has built for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God cannot be insensible, dishonorable, or powerless; settling people in this providential world is a test that ends in gathering, disclosure of deeds, reward, and punishment.
rows.anchor: by settling these inhabitants in this house, He wants to test and try them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic questions about how signs were made or raised are concise; other sūrahs elaborate, and a full account requires examining the Qur'an's related passages.
rows.anchor: are very concise and brief.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sign sequence moves from the familiar camel upward to the sky, down to intervening mountains, and then naturally to the outspread earth, leaving the stubborn no excuse.
rows.anchor: the stubborn are left with no excuse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Camel and earth chiefly display providence, while sky and mountains display power and wisdom; these attributes underpin the Hereafter and recompense.
rows.anchor: the camel and the earth, are prominent with regard to providence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After presenting the arguments, the discourse turns to the Prophet: deniers lack fear rather than evidence, and only the God-fearing benefit from the signs.
rows.anchor: the discourse shifts and addresses the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should persist in preaching and reminding regardless of results; his duty is not to make people embrace faith, and God will not hold him responsible for their rejection.
rows.anchor: his responsibility is only to preach and remind people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Context supplies omitted words before illā: those receptive to guidance benefit, whereas those who turn away and deny face severe punishment.
rows.anchor: a suppression of some words has occurred which can be determined through contextual indications.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greatest punishment is Hell, greater than any worldly torment in extent or duration; al-Aʿlā calls it the great fire without changing the meaning.
rows.anchor: the torment of Hell which will be the greatest among the torments of this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Return to God and His accounting are indubitable; without judgment this world would be purposeless, contrary to its wise Creator.
rows.anchor: its Creator does nothing which is bereft of wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlaq counterparts al-Tīn: both center salvation on faith and righteous deeds, while those rejecting this path bring doom upon themselves.
rows.anchor: the real path of salvation is that he should profess faith and do righteous deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh and its leaders take the opposite path, rejecting the revealed guide through arrogance and even trying to stop the Messenger praying.
rows.anchor: they have chosen to go on the opposite path.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to recite in the name of the Lord who created; human creation from a clot shows re-creation is possible, and pen and writing taught unlettered people what they did not know.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has created man from a clot of congealed blood and He also has full power to re-create him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders' pride in wealth and status makes them indifferent to God despite their eventual accounting before Him.
rows.anchor: one day everyone shall be called to account before Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those stopping the Prophet from prayer are sharply challenged to consider whether he is guided and urges piety while they reject him, then warned to contemplate their fate.
rows.anchor: The haughty who would stop the Prophet (sws) from praying are especially warned and threatened.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse's fury increases: God observes the rebels, and if they persist He will drag them by their forelocks.
rows.anchor: More rage and fury is expressed at the attitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning says God sees the rebels' insolence and will seize them by their forelocks if they do not desist.
rows.anchor: the Almighty is observing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should persevere, forbear, disregard the rebels' provocations, prostrate, and draw near to God.
rows.anchor: show perseverance and forbearance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqraʾ can be a teacher's instruction to read, but it can also direct someone to read or recite aloud to others.
rows.anchor: is not merely used to convey what a teacher would say to a student

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 7:204 and 17:45 show that iqraʾ can mean reciting the Qur'an aloud to an audience; the usage is indicated by these verses.
rows.anchor: The indication to this usage is present within the verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reciting in the Creator's name presents the Qur'an as God's binding directive, not a preacher's words or a request; people must obey and not mock or trivialize it.
rows.anchor: what is being recited out to them is directly from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an is uniquely composed entirely of words revealed by God, so its opponents should recognize its exaltedness and fear its wrath.
rows.anchor: No other Book before it has the honour to be entirely composed of the words revealed by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier scriptures predict that Muhammad would speak in God's name and that God would hold accountable those rejecting his message.
rows.anchor: whatever he will say, he will say in the name of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human creation verse specifies the general mention of creation in verse 1.
rows.anchor: This is an expression of the specific after the general.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlaq means a clot of congealed blood, recalling embryonic stages also discussed in al-Ḥajj, al-Muʾminūn, al-Sajdah, al-Qiyāmah, and al-Dahr.
rows.anchor: a clot of congealed blood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human development displays God's power and wisdom, making resurrection possible; it also shows purposeful creation that entails accountability for deeds.
rows.anchor: He fashions out a living being having such faculties

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being made from trivial material gives no grounds for pride, self-glorification, or self-veneration.
rows.anchor: man who has been created from such trivial and inconsequential stuff to show conceit and pride

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the context invokes God's power to recreate and hold humanity accountable: the Prophet must present God's Book and remind them who made them from a clot.
rows.anchor: should present the Book of God specifically in His name
